one_liner: ~450-line in-situ C++11 JSON DOM parser, 1.2-1.5x faster than default RapidJSON on kostya's number-heavy JSON test.
what_it_does: gason parses a writable, NUL-terminated char buffer into a read-only tree with one call. jsonParse(source, &endptr, &value, allocator) returns an error code and fills in a JsonValue. Values expose getTag(), toNumber(), toString() and toNode(). You walk arrays and objects with range-for over JsonNode* items, and object nodes also carry a key. It has no random access, key lookup, mutation or serializer, so it does not replace RapidJSON: the API is different and it only parses and reads.
how_it_is_fast: It parses destructively in place. Strings are unescaped and NUL-terminated inside the source buffer and referenced by pointer, so string data is never copied. Every value is an 8-byte NaN-boxed double: numbers are stored as raw doubles, and every other type is a 4-bit tag plus a 47-bit pointer. Array and object members are singly-linked nodes of 16 or 24 bytes, taken from a bump-pointer zone allocator (4 KiB malloc'd blocks) and freed all at once. The parser is one non-recursive switch loop with a fixed 32-entry container stack. It converts numbers with a hand-rolled digit accumulator instead of strtod, which is fast but not correctly rounded.
when_to_use: Parsing trusted JSON once when it already sits in a writable buffer you can give up, and a sequential walk of the tree is enough (for example, pulling fields or sums from a large data dump or config).
Number-heavy documents where approximate doubles are acceptable. kostya's generated file of 524,288 coordinate objects is this shape, and gason took 0.127 s there vs 0.154 s for RapidJSON (g++).
Memory-constrained parsing. In the same test, gason's RSS grew by 96.75 MiB, vs 123.44 MiB for RapidJSON, 175.86 MiB for simdjson DOM and 229.38 MiB for yyjson (g++/gcc).
Projects that want a tiny vendored parser: two files, about 450 lines, no dependencies, builds with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti, on x86-64 or 32-bit targets.
when_not_to_use: Untrusted or validation-critical input. It accepts invalid JSON (trailing commas, {"a" null}, leading zeros, 0e, ["x"]]) and passes only 25 of 34 nativejson-benchmark validation cases. Open issue #43 (2026) reports reads past the terminating NUL when whitespace comes right before it, and the source confirms that path.

When numbers must be exact. Conversion is not correctly rounded: it passes 26 of 66 nativejson-benchmark double tests, 5e-324 parses as 0 and 1.7976931348623157e308 as inf. There is no integer type, so integers above 2^53 lose precision.

Platforms with tagged or wide pointers, such as Android on aarch64 with tagged heap pointers. NaN-boxing keeps only 47 pointer bits, so the type tag gets corrupted (open issue #36, seen on a Pixel 5). The guarding assert is compiled out in release builds, so the failure is silent.

Documents nested more than 32 levels deep: the stack size is fixed and the parse returns JSON_STACK_OVERFLOW. Also skip it when you need keyed or indexed access, DOM editing or JSON output; none of these exist, and objects are linear lists.
When peak speed matters most: simdjson On-Demand (0.060 s), DAW JSON Link (0.089 s) and simdjson DOM (0.107 s) all beat gason's 0.127 s in the same kostya test.

integration.min_toolchain: C++11. VS2012 fails to compile it (open issue #22); VS2013 and later are reported to work. kostya builds it with g++ 16.1 and clang++ 22.1.8 at -std=c++23.
integration.platforms: 64-bit targets whose pointers fit in 47 bits (typical x86-64) and 32-bit targets (fixed in 2015). Broken on aarch64 with tagged heap pointers, e.g. Android (issue #36).
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. In the source, jsonParse keeps no global state: all parser state lives on the stack or in the caller's JsonAllocator. Concurrent parses with separate buffers and allocators should therefore be safe, but that is inferred, not stated.

gotchas: The source buffer is overwritten, and every string points into it. Keep the buffer and the JsonAllocator alive for as long as you use any JsonValue; destroying the allocator invalidates the whole tree.
Array nodes are allocated without the key field, so reading node->key while iterating an array reads garbage. The README says only next and value are valid for arrays, and issue #38 hit this.
Strings are C strings: \u0000 truncates them, and a surrogate pair such as \uD834\uDD1E becomes two 3-byte sequences, which is invalid UTF-8. Raw non-ASCII bytes are not validated.

There is no length parameter, so the input must be NUL-terminated. Parsing stops after the first complete value and endptr points at the rest, so trailing data is not an error unless you check endptr yourself.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: In kostya's test, simdjson is faster (On-Demand 0.060 s, DOM 0.107 s) and yyjson roughly ties gason (0.131 s vs 0.127 s). kostya flags gason's number parsing as inaccurate but not theirs, so choose gason only when a two-file, ~450-line vendorable parser with a smaller tree (96.75 MiB RSS growth vs 175-229 MiB) matters more than exact numbers, strict validation and maintenance.
verified_claims_summary: kostya/benchmarks (README update 2026-07-19; Intel Xeon E-2324G, Debian Docker, -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c++23) parsed a generated file of 524,288 coordinate objects and averaged x/y/z. gason took 0.127 s vs 0.154 s for RapidJSON's default DOM Parse() with g++ 16.1 (1.21x), and 0.133 s vs 0.194 s with clang++ 22.1.8/libc++ (1.46x); gason parses in place, while the RapidJSON test copies strings and no ParseInsitu variant was run. The author's 2013-14 shootout against 2013 RapidJSON trunk (i7, clang-500) is mixed: gason is 2.4x faster on monster.json (924 vs 2210 us) but slower on big.json (20092 vs 18093 us).
status_note: Abandoned: the last code fix was in 2016 and the last commit, in 2021, merged a typo fix, while 11 issues stay open, including tagged-pointer breakage, inexact numbers and an out-of-bounds read; it is MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor and patch yourself.
